title: FIR Filters, FFT Convolution and Wavelets
description: Ten original questions on filter ideals, window design, linear phase, FFT convolution, STFT resolution, Haar DWT and translation invariance. Multiple-response scoring is for practice only: +1 per correct selection and -0.5 per incorrect selection, floored at zero. Includes Kaiser order estimation and explicitly normalized Haar coefficient calculations.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish ideal low-pass and high-pass filters?

options.content: An ideal high-pass filter suppresses frequencies near DC.
An ideal low-pass filter passes frequencies near DC.
They have identical magnitude responses at every frequency.
Both are described by passband and stopband regions separated by a cutoff in the ideal model.

questions.explanation: Low-pass and high-pass filters select complementary low- and high-frequency regions. Their ideal responses change abruptly at a cutoff, though practical designs require a transition band.

questions.prompt: Why can an ideal brick-wall frequency response not be implemented exactly as a finite, causal FIR filter?

options.content: A zero-phase ideal response produces a two-sided impulse response.
The window method approximates the ideal response by shifting and windowing a finite portion of its impulse response.
A finite number of taps can reproduce an arbitrary discontinuous ideal response exactly.
Its inverse transform has an impulse response extending infinitely in time.

questions.explanation: A nontrivial brick-wall response has frequency discontinuities and an infinite-duration sinc-like inverse transform. No finite impulse response can reproduce it exactly. The window method shifts and windows a finite portion, introducing transition width and ripple; this is one FIR design method, not a requirement that every FIR design algorithm use truncation.
questions.source: EE3731C ClassicalSignal3Questions.pdf, page 1, Q1; EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal2_condensed.pdf, slides 35-49

questions.prompt: In the window method for FIR design, which trade-offs are generally relevant?

options.content: A longer window can produce a narrower transition band.
Abrupt rectangular truncation tends to produce stronger sidelobes than smoother windows.
Window choice affects sidelobe level and passband or stopband ripple.
Window length and shape have no effect on the realized frequency response.

questions.explanation: Longer filters improve frequency resolution, while smoother windows reduce sidelobes at the cost of a broader mainlobe. The window therefore controls transition width and ripple together.

questions.prompt: A low-pass Kaiser design targets attenuation $A=60\ \mathrm{dB}$ and transition width $\Delta\omega=0.2\pi$. Use $\beta=0.1102(A-8.7)$ and round $M=(A-8)/(2.285\Delta\omega)$ upward. Which statements are correct?

options.content: $\beta\approx5.65$.
The estimated filter order is M=37.
The resulting coefficient count is 38.
The window parameter β is 60 because it equals attenuation in dB.
The estimated order is 38 because order equals the coefficient count.
Using 0.2 instead of 0.2π for Δω leaves the estimated order unchanged.

questions.explanation: Substitution gives $\beta=5.65326$ and $52/(2.285\times0.2\pi)\approx36.22$, rounded up to order 37 and length M+1=38. The width is in radians per sample. These empirical estimates need a response check; if the target were high-pass with nonzero Nyquist gain, symmetric Type II would be unsuitable and the order would need to be even.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal3_condensed.pdf, slides 10-12 and 21; EE3731C ClassicalSignal3Questions.pdf, page 1, Q2

questions.prompt: Which coefficient condition gives the real symmetric Type I and Type II FIR filters discussed in the lecture their generalized linear phase?

options.content: The real coefficients satisfy $h[n]=h[M-n]$ about the midpoint M/2.
The coefficients are independent random values.
Every coefficient is strictly positive.
The impulse response has infinite duration.

questions.explanation: For order M, symmetry $h[n]=h[M-n]$ lets the response be written $H(e^{j\omega})=e^{-j\omega M/2}A(\omega)$ with real A. Type I has even M; Type II has odd M. Sign changes of A can add phase jumps of π. Positivity alone does not impose symmetry, and FIR coefficients are finite in number.

questions.prompt: Sequences have lengths $L_x$ and $L_h$. Which statements about FFT-based convolution are correct?

options.content: Their full linear convolution has length $L_x+L_h-1$.
After padding, multiply the DFTs and take the inverse DFT.
Using a DFT length at least $L_x+L_h-1$ avoids time-domain aliasing.
Without sufficient padding, circular convolution is always identical to full linear convolution.

questions.explanation: DFT multiplication produces circular convolution. Padding to at least the linear-convolution length prevents wraparound overlap, so the inverse DFT equals the desired linear result.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal3_condensed.pdf, slides 32-55; EE3731C ClassicalSignal3Questions.pdf, pages 1-2, Q4

questions.prompt: What distinctions between STFT and wavelet analysis are illustrated by the diagram?

image.alt: Time increases to the right and frequency upward. STFT tiles have uniform width and height. Wavelet tiles are narrow in time and tall in frequency at high frequencies, and wide in time and short in frequency at low frequencies; all schematic tile areas are equal.

options.content: A fixed STFT window gives one time-frequency resolution across the plane.
Both methods provide arbitrarily fine time and frequency resolution simultaneously.
Coarser time resolution can be paired with finer frequency resolution at low frequencies.
Wavelets use multiple scales and therefore multiresolution analysis.

questions.explanation: A single STFT window fixes the cell shape. Wavelet scale changes provide short windows at high frequency and long windows at low frequency. Neither method escapes the fundamental time-frequency resolution trade-off.

questions.prompt: For x=[3,7,8,2], define one-level orthonormal Haar pairs by $a_k=(x[2k]+x[2k+1])/\sqrt2$ and $d_k=(x[2k]-x[2k+1])/\sqrt2$. No thresholding is applied. Which statements are correct?

options.content: Downsampling halves the total energy to 63 despite the stated normalization.
Under the stated convention, $d=[2\sqrt2,-3\sqrt2]$.
The sum of squared coefficients is 126, equal to the input energy.
The approximation coefficients alone determine all four original samples uniquely.
$a=[5\sqrt2,5\sqrt2]$.

questions.explanation: The pair sums are 10 and 10; differences are -4 and 6. Division by √2 gives the listed coefficients. Input energy is $9+49+64+4=126$ and coefficient energy is $50+50+8+18=126$. The opposite detail signs use a different convention. Exact reconstruction needs both branches: $x[2k]=(a_k+d_k)/\sqrt2$, $x[2k+1]=(a_k-d_k)/\sqrt2$.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal4_condensed.pdf, slides 20-29; EE3731C ClassicalSignal4Questions.pdf, page 1, Q1

questions.prompt: A critically sampled DWT is generally not translation invariant because shifting the input can change which samples survive each downsampling step.

options.content: True
False

questions.explanation: Downsampling ties the coefficients to a sampling phase. Even a one-sample input shift can produce a very different coefficient pattern, motivating stationary or cycle-spun alternatives.

questions.prompt: Which steps belong to a spin-cycle wavelet procedure?

options.content: It always uses fewer coefficients and less computation than one ordinary DWT.
Circularly shift the input by several offsets.
Apply the wavelet-domain operation to each shifted version.
Invert each shift after reconstruction and average the results.

questions.explanation: Cycle spinning repeats the transform over multiple circular shifts, undoes the shifts and averages. This reduces shift sensitivity but creates an overcomplete and more computationally expensive procedure.
questions.source: EE3731C Yeo_ClassicalSignal4_condensed.pdf, slides 41-44; EE3731C ClassicalSignal4Questions.pdf, page 1, Q1
